How a rope ferry crosses

A rope ferry crosses a river without an engine, using the current itself. The boat hangs from a cable strung bank to bank, and the ferryman sets its angle against the flow. The water pushes on the angled hull and the cable stops it from being swept downstream.

Sidebar: chain ferries and cable cars.

The crossing takes longer at low water, when the current has less to give, and the angle is increased to make up the difference. On a slack river the boat has to be pulled across hand over hand.

Search the ferry notes.

The cable is the whole machine. It sags out of the way of anything coming downstream and holds a loaded boat against the current, and the tension is adjusted every season as the banks move.

Region note: the cable sags on purpose.
